post_title: Why People Seek Help, and What They Actually Need From It
post_content:
There is a gap between why someone walks into a helping relationship and what they actually need once they are there. In more than four decades of teaching and researching the helping process, I have come to believe that closing that gap is the real work of the skilled helper. Most people arrive carrying a story. What they need is someone willing to help them understand it.

#### What Brings Someone to a Helper

The reasons people seek help are rarely as straightforward as they appear. A person might say they are struggling with anxiety, or a relationship breakdown, or a career that no longer makes sense. And all of that is true. But underneath the presenting concern, there is almost always something less named: a sense that they are stuck in a pattern they cannot see clearly enough to change.

People seek help, in my experience, not because they are broken, but because they have reached the limit of what they can do alone. That is not a failure. It is a remarkably human recognition.

Most of us can sustain our own navigation through familiar territory. When the terrain shifts and the old maps stop working, we look for someone who can help us read the ground.

The mistake a helper can make at this point is to rush toward solving the problem as it was presented. The presenting problem is rarely the whole story. It is the door. What the client actually needs is someone willing to open it with them, not someone who has already decided what is on the other side.

Consider a man who arrives saying he wants help managing his temper at work. That is a real problem and it deserves attention.

But if the helper begins there, with techniques for managing anger, they may never learn that the temper appeared eighteen months ago, that it coincided with a promotion he did not want and could not refuse, and that what he is actually living with is a slow, unspoken sense that he has agreed to a life he did not choose. The anger is a symptom of something the man himself has not yet put into words. A helper who solves the presenting problem here has solved the wrong problem competently.

#### The Three Things Clients Are Usually Asking For

Across a great many helping relationships, I have come to think that what people are asking for, underneath whatever they say, tends to fall into three categories, and it is useful for a helper to know which one is in the room.

The first is clarity. The person cannot see their own situation well enough to act on it. Too many things are tangled together, or one thing is so large that it obscures everything around it. What they need is not advice but the experience of laying it out in front of someone who will help them see the shape of it.

The second is permission. The person often already knows what they want to do, and what they lack is the sense that it is legitimate to want it. This is more common than most helpers expect.

They are not looking for a decision. They are looking for the experience of saying the thing out loud to someone who does not immediately argue them out of it.

The third is capability. The person knows what they want and believes they are allowed to want it, and genuinely does not know how to get there. This is the only one of the three where anything resembling instruction is appropriate, and it is the least common of the three at the point of first contact, though helpers frequently treat it as the default.

Reading which of these is present, and not assuming, is one of the more consequential judgements in early helping.

#### What Clients Actually Need

If I had to name the one thing clients need from a helper, it would be this: the experience of being genuinely understood before anything else happens.

Not reassured. Not advised. Not redirected. Understood.

There is a passage in *The Skilled Helper* where I describe what a good helper makes possible: not the heroic intervention, not the transformative breakthrough, but the quieter thing, which is a relationship in which the client feels safe enough to look honestly at their own situation. That safety is not a soft precondition to the real work. It is the real work, in its early and most critical form.

Clients who feel understood are more likely to explore honestly. They are more willing to surface the things they have been avoiding, to name the beliefs that are keeping them stuck, to consider possibilities they had ruled out.

The client who feels managed or assessed or corrected tends to do the opposite. They perform. They present the version of themselves they think the helper wants to see.

This is why I hold the view that empathy is not a therapeutic technique. It is a stance, and it shapes everything that follows.

#### Why This Matters for How We Help

If what clients need first is to be understood, then the helper's primary discipline in the early stages of any helping relationship is not problem-solving. It is careful, unhurried listening, and the ability to communicate what has been heard in a way that shows the client they have been met.

This has practical consequences. A helper who moves too quickly to action planning, who introduces goals before the client's story has been properly heard, will often find that the action plan does not stick. Not because the plan is wrong, but because the client did not feel understood well enough to fully own it.

It also changes how a helper thinks about time. A session spent entirely on exploration, with no plan produced and no action agreed, can look from the outside like a session in which nothing happened. It is frequently the session that makes everything after it possible. Helpers under pressure to demonstrate progress are pushed toward the visible and away from the foundational, and the cost of that pressure is usually paid three or four sessions later, when a well-designed plan quietly fails to be enacted.

The structure I have described in *The Skilled Helper* is not a system to follow mechanically. It is a map for a human process. The map is useful precisely because it keeps the helper oriented toward the client's needs rather than their own need to feel helpful.

#### What to Do With This

If you are working as a helper, or developing toward that work, I would invite you to sit with one question: in your recent helping conversations, how much time passed before you moved from listening to advising?

Not because advising is always wrong. But because the ratio often reveals where the pressure is. When we move quickly, it is frequently our discomfort with sitting in another person's uncertainty, rather than a genuine signal that the client is ready to move.

The discipline of slowing down, of staying with the client's experience a little longer than feels comfortable, is one of the most transferable skills in this work. It is also, in my observation, one of the least practiced. It costs nothing to try in your next conversation, and it tends to reveal quickly how much you had been supplying that the other person had not asked for.

Over 3,600 students have worked through it, and it sits within [the School of Life Coaching and Professional Helping](/academy/life-coaching/).

post_title: Listening Is Not Waiting to Speak: The Discipline of Tuning In
post_content:
Most people who enter a helping role believe they are good listeners. My experience, after a lifetime of training helpers and studying the helping process, is that most of us are not nearly as good at it as we think. Listening well is one of the most demanding disciplines in human communication, and it is almost never taught.

#### What Listening Actually Requires

When I describe listening in *The Skilled Helper*, I use the phrase tuning in. Not because it is poetic, but because it names something precise. Tuning in means attending to the whole person, not only the words. It means tracking the feelings behind the language, the things being avoided as well as the things being said, the way a sentence trails off or a topic is abandoned.

Most helpers listen at the level of content. They hear what is said and begin forming a response.

What they miss is the register. They miss the slight hesitation before a particular word. They miss the way energy drops when a subject is raised. They miss the moment when someone stops telling their story and starts performing it.

Listening at this level takes practice, and it takes something else too: the willingness to hold your own response in reserve. The urge to reply is strong. For many of us in helping roles, it is connected to something that feels like care, because we want to be useful, and responding feels like usefulness. But the discipline of tuning in asks something harder: to stay with the client's experience rather than moving toward our own.

#### The Three Layers of What Is Being Said

It helps to think of any client's account as arriving in three layers, each of which can be listened to and any of which can be missed.

The first layer is the content: the events, the people, the sequence of what happened. This is the layer almost everyone hears, and it is the layer most helpers can accurately summarise afterwards.

The second layer is the feeling: what the events meant to the person, what they are still carrying about them, what emotion sits underneath the recounting. This layer is often not stated directly. It appears in emphasis, in what gets repeated, in what is described in unusual detail and what is skipped over quickly. A person who describes a difficult meeting minute by minute and then says "and then I went home" in four words has told you where the weight is.

The third layer is the meaning the person has made: the conclusion they have drawn about themselves, about others, or about what is possible. This is the layer that most often needs revisiting, and it is the layer least likely to be volunteered, because the person does not experience it as an interpretation. They experience it as what the events proved.

A helper listening only at the first layer will produce accurate summaries and change very little. A helper who can hear all three has something to work with.

#### What Gets in the Way

There are three things I observe most often getting in the way of genuine listening.

The first is premature understanding. We form an interpretation of what the client means, and once we have formed it, we stop truly listening. Everything that follows is filtered through the interpretation we have already arrived at. A helper in this state is no longer attending to the client; they are confirming their own hypothesis.

The second is advice readiness. The moment a problem becomes legible, many helpers begin composing a response. The listening becomes a formality.

The client senses this, usually without being able to name it, and the result is a subtle withdrawal. They say less, and they say it less honestly.

The third is distraction by one's own experience. A client describes a situation that echoes something in the helper's own life, and the helper is suddenly partly elsewhere, partly managing their own material.

This is not a character fault. It is a human reflex. But it costs the client the quality of attention they came for.

#### What It Looks Like to Listen Well

A helper who is genuinely tuned in communicates that they are present. Not through technique, not through careful paraphrasing performed for effect, but through the quality of their attention. The client feels met, not observed.

Concretely, it means maintaining the kind of contact that invites the client to keep going. It means resisting the urge to finish sentences, to redirect, to insert your own frame over the one the client is building. It means allowing silence, because silence is often where the important material lives.

And it means responding in a way that shows you have heard not only the content but the feeling. Not by labelling the feeling for the client, which can feel presumptuous, but by reflecting what you have heard in a way that gives the client room to confirm or correct it.

There is a particular kind of silence worth learning to recognise. It is the pause that comes after a person has said something slightly more honest than they intended. It is short, and it is fragile, and the most common thing a helper does with it is fill it. Left alone, it is very often followed by the most useful sentence in the conversation.

#### Why This Cannot Be Faked

Helpers are sometimes taught listening as a set of visible behaviours: maintain eye contact, nod, paraphrase what you heard, do not interrupt. Each of those correlates with genuine attention, which is why they were noticed in the first place. None of them produces it.

A person performing the behaviours of listening while mentally composing their reply is a familiar experience to almost everyone who has been on the receiving end of it, and the giveaway is rarely anything you could point at. It is the quality of what comes back. A reply that was formed while you were still speaking answers the version of your problem that existed thirty seconds ago, and it lands slightly off, in a way that is hard to articulate and easy to feel.

This matters practically because it means listening cannot be improved by adding techniques on top of divided attention. The technique is downstream. What has to change is what you are doing with your own mind while the other person speaks, and the honest starting point is noticing how much of that time is currently spent on your own contribution.

There is a modest exercise that reveals this quickly. In your next conversation, resolve that you will not speak until you have silently named, to yourself, what the other person is feeling. Not what you think of it, not what you would suggest. Just the feeling.

Most people find they cannot do it, because they had not been tracking that at all.

#### What to Do With This

The clearest diagnostic I know is this: after a helping conversation, ask yourself how much you remember of what the client said, and how much you remember of what you said. If the balance tilts toward your own contributions, you were probably listening less well than you believed.

A second, harder test: can you name what the person felt, as distinct from what happened to them? If the only account you can give is a sequence of events, you heard the first layer and missed the two beneath it.

Developing genuine listening is slow work, and it requires honest self-observation. post_title: What Clients Hear When a Helper Responds With Real Empathy
post_content:
Empathy is one of the most used words in the helping professions and one of the least examined. In my experience, the helpers who describe themselves as empathic are not always the ones their clients experience that way. What a helper intends to communicate and what a client actually receives are two different things, and the gap between them is where much helping fails.

#### What Empathy Is and Is Not

I want to be precise about this, because precision matters. Empathy, as I understand and teach it, is not sympathy. Sympathy is what happens when you feel something for a person. Empathy is what happens when you communicate that you understand what a person feels, and that you understand it from the inside, from their frame of reference, not your own.

The distinction is not academic. A response that comes from sympathy says, in effect, I feel something about your situation. A response that comes from empathy says, I understand something about your experience of your situation.

The client does not need you to feel what they feel. They need you to demonstrate that you can see the world as they are seeing it, even temporarily, even imperfectly.

In *The Skilled Helper*, I describe this as communicating a perception, not a verdict. When a helper reflects what they have understood about a client's experience, they are offering a perception. The client then has the opportunity to confirm it, refine it, or correct it. That process, of offering and receiving and correcting, is itself part of the healing.

It is worth adding that empathy is not agreement, and helpers new to this often confuse the two. You can understand precisely why a person feels justified in an action you think was unwise, and communicate that understanding fully, without endorsing the action. Indeed the understanding is what makes it possible to examine the action later. A helper who withholds empathy because they disapprove has closed the only door through which the disapproved-of behaviour might eventually be looked at honestly.

#### What Clients Actually Hear

Clients who experience real empathy from a helper tend to describe it in a consistent way, even when they use different words. They say things like: I felt understood. They say: it was the first time I had been able to put it into words. They say: I did not feel judged.

What they are describing is the experience of being met. And being met changes something. It changes the client's relationship to their own experience. When something that has felt heavy or shameful or confused is received without alarm, without correction, without redirection, it becomes slightly more possible to look at it.

This is not a mystical process. It has a mechanism. When the client perceives that the helper has understood accurately, and that the understanding has not frightened or repulsed or bored the helper, the client gains a degree of distance from the experience they have been too close to. They can begin to see it rather than only live inside it.

There is a second effect, less often noticed. A person who has been accurately understood by someone else becomes better at understanding themselves. The helper's reflection gives them language they did not have, and language is what makes an experience examinable rather than merely endured.

Over a series of conversations, clients frequently begin to produce for themselves the kind of reflection the helper had been offering. That is not imitation. It is the capacity transferring.

#### The Common Failures

The most common failure is labelling rather than reflecting. A helper who tells a client what they are feeling, rather than communicating what they have heard the client feel, has substituted their own interpretation for the client's experience. This often shuts down rather than opens up.

The second failure is a reflection that is technically accurate but emotionally thin. It names the content of what was said but not the weight of it. The client hears the words reflected back and does not feel understood, because what mattered was not the content but the significance of it.

The third failure, which I think is underappreciated, is accuracy without permission. A helper who reflects something true but that the client was not yet ready to hear has moved ahead of where the client is. Empathy at the wrong moment, however accurate, can close rather than open.

There is a fourth worth naming, because it is well-intentioned and therefore hard to see: empathy offered as reassurance. The helper hears distress and responds by minimising it, out of a genuine wish to relieve the person.

Anyone would feel that way. It is not as bad as it seems. You have handled worse. Each of these may be true, and each of them tells the client that the feeling they brought was slightly too much, and should be reduced before it can be received.

#### Empathy Under Pressure

Everything above is straightforward in a calm conversation with someone whose situation is legible and whose distress is proportionate. It becomes considerably harder in three situations worth naming, because these are where helpers most often lose the stance without noticing.

The first is when the client's account seems unfair to someone who is not in the room. The instinct to defend the absent party is strong, particularly in a helper who values even-handedness. But the client is not asking for a verdict on the other person, and a helper who supplies one has stopped attending to the client's experience in order to correct their conclusion.

The second is when the distress seems disproportionate to the event. It is worth remembering that you are hearing a fragment of a history you do not have. What looks like an overreaction to a small thing is very often an accurate reaction to a long pattern, of which the small thing is the latest instalment.

The third is when the client is describing something the helper has strong feelings about from their own life. The temptation here is not to withdraw but to over-identify: to feel that you understand immediately and completely, because you have been there. You have been somewhere superficially similar. Assuming the rest is one of the fastest routes to a client feeling profoundly unheard while the helper believes the opposite.

#### What to Do With This

The practice of empathy is the practice of noticing what you have heard and asking yourself, before you respond: am I reflecting what the client said, or what I think the client meant? Is my response in their language or mine? Does it leave room for them to correct me?

Those questions, asked honestly before each response, change the quality of what comes back.

A useful way to test yourself is to notice how often the person you are helping says some version of "yes, and". A reflection that lands accurately tends to be met with confirmation followed by more material: yes, and the other thing is. A reflection that has missed tends to be met with correction, or with a polite yes followed by nothing.

The second response is not a failure. It is information, offered freely, and the helper's job is to take it and try again.

post_title: The Blind Spots That Keep Good People Stuck in Old Patterns
post_content:
The people who come to helpers are not, in the main, people who lack intelligence or effort. Most have tried many things. Most have thought about their situations carefully, often obsessively.

And yet the pattern they are caught in continues. Understanding why requires looking at something that intelligence alone cannot correct: the blind spot.

#### What a Blind Spot Is

A blind spot, in the context of helping, is not a gap in knowledge. It is a gap in perspective. It is something that is true about a person's situation that they cannot currently see, not because the information is hidden, but because their way of seeing has organised itself in a way that makes it invisible.

I have observed, across many years of teaching and research, that blind spots are not random. They cluster around the things that matter most. A person is most likely to be blind in precisely the areas where insight would require a significant and costly change.

The blindness is not accidental. In some functional sense it is protective, though the protection comes at the price of freedom.

In *The Skilled Helper*, I describe this as the difference between a client's story as told and the fuller story beneath it. The told story is almost always coherent. It usually assigns cause and effect in a way that makes the client the reasonable person in the situation. The fuller story, when it eventually becomes accessible, tends to be more complicated, more implicating, and more useful.

#### The Shapes Blind Spots Take

It is worth being concrete about the forms these take, because naming them makes them easier to notice.

The most common is the unexamined role. A person describes a repeating situation in which they are consistently the one responding to what others do. Their colleague is difficult, their partner withdraws, their manager is unreasonable. The account may be accurate in every particular and still leave out the person's own contribution, not because they are hiding it but because from inside their own experience they were only ever reacting.

A second is the outdated conclusion. Something was learned in a context that no longer exists and has never been revisited. A person who was genuinely powerless at twenty-two operates at forty as though the same constraints apply, and the constraint they are living under is the memory rather than the situation.

A third is the protected good. A person will not examine an area because examining it might require giving something up that they are not willing to lose. This is the most sensitive of the three, and the one that most rewards patience, because pushing at it directly tends to produce not insight but a firmer defence.

#### How Blind Spots Survive

A blind spot survives through two mechanisms. The first is selective attention: the client notices the evidence that confirms their existing understanding and does not notice, or does not weigh equally, the evidence that disrupts it.

This is not dishonesty. It is how human perception works. We see what we are primed to see.

The second mechanism is the story the client has told many times. Every retelling reinforces the same structure, the same interpretations, the same conclusion about who did what and why. A story told often enough becomes a fact, and facts are not available for examination in the way that stories are.

The helper's task is not to challenge the story. It is to help the client become curious about it.

#### How a Helper Can Help

The key move here is what I call challenging, and I mean that word carefully. A challenge in helping is not a confrontation. It is an invitation to see something the client is not currently seeing, offered with the care that comes from genuine understanding.

A challenge that arrives without understanding behind it tends to produce defensiveness. The client hears the challenge as an accusation, or as evidence that the helper has misunderstood, and they retreat into the told story more firmly than before. This is why challenge is something that follows the establishment of real contact and real understanding, never something that precedes it.

Done well, a challenge sounds like genuine curiosity. It asks the client to look again at something they thought they understood. It does so without suggesting that they have been wrong, but by opening a small gap in the story through which new light can enter.

One reliable route in is the discrepancy. Where a person's own account contains two things that do not quite fit together, the helper does not have to supply an outside perspective at all. They can simply hold both parts up and ask about the space between them.

You have said this matters more to you than anything, and also that you have not had time for it in two years. I am curious about how those sit together for you.

Nothing has been asserted. The client's own material has been offered back, and the examination is theirs to do. That is why the discrepancy works where a direct observation does not.

#### Why Simply Pointing It Out Does Not Work

It is worth explaining why the direct route fails, because it looks so efficient that most helpers try it at least once.

If a blind spot were an information gap, telling the person would close it. But a blind spot is held in place by something, and the something is usually the cost of seeing. Telling a person what they cannot see does not remove that cost. It presents the bill without warning, from someone who is not paying it.

What follows is predictable. The person defends, and the defence is not dishonest; from inside their frame the helper's observation genuinely looks wrong. And because they have now argued the position out loud, they hold it slightly more firmly than before. The intervention has strengthened what it was meant to loosen.

There is a second cost, which is to the relationship. A helper who names something before the person is ready to see it has demonstrated that they will do that, and the person adjusts what they bring accordingly. Material that might have surfaced in a month does not surface at all.

The slower route is not a matter of politeness. It is the only route that works, because insight that arrives from outside is information, and insight that arrives from inside is a change of view. Only the second one alters anything.

#### What to Do With This

In your own situations, the question worth sitting with is this: where in my life do I have a story that has not changed in a long time? Not because the circumstances are unchangeable, but because the interpretation is fixed. That fixed interpretation is where the blind spot is most likely to live.

A second question, which most people find more uncomfortable: what would I have to give up if I were wrong about this? Where the answer is nothing much, the interpretation is probably fine. Where the answer is something substantial, you have found the place worth looking.

Challenging blind spots in yourself and in others is one of the core competencies the [Skilled Helper Practitioner Course (Advanced to Expert)](/academy/life-coaching/skilled-helper-practitioner/) is built around.
